title: CO next-hour prediction - Italy (UCI Air Quality)
summary: We predicted CO one hour ahead using the Italy (UCI Air Quality) data. XGBoost did best on the validation period, so we used it. On the test period (16 Jan 2005 to 4 Apr 2005) its average error was 0.391 mg/m³. Just repeating the last hour's value gave 0.519 mg/m³, so the model was 24.7% better. 27 episodes were flagged: 17 look like unusual pollution, 5 look like data problems and 5 are unclear. Its prediction was within 20% of the real value in 61% of the test hours. No sign of overfitting: the error on new data is close to the error on the data it learned from.
how_it_was_made: Read the hourly data and treated empty cells and -200 as missing.

Built the inputs: hour, weekday, the reading 1 hour before, the reading 2 hours before, the reading 3 hours before, the reading at the same time the day before, temperature, relative humidity, absolute humidity.
Split the timeline in order: first 60% to train, next 20% to choose the model, last 20% to test.
Tried Linear Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost, each with a few settings that keep it from memorising the training hours. Each predicts how much the level changes in the next hour.
Checked for overfitting: compared the chosen model's average error on the hours it learned from with its error on the test hours, allowing for some periods being harder to predict than others.

Counted the test hours where the prediction was within 20% of the real value. Readings below the 10th percentile were measured against that percentile, so tiny misses on near-zero readings don't count as big ones.
Flagged test hours where the miss was more than 1.71 mg/m³ (bigger than 95% of the misses on the validation period).
By design this limit flags 5% of the validation hours; on the test period it flagged 2.0% of hours. So the number of episodes partly depends on where the limit is set.

Grouped flagged hours that were less than 3 hours apart and checked each group: missing inputs or a gap, a stuck reading, or a sudden jump that nothing else shared mean a data problem; other pollutants moving the same way at the same time mean unusual pollution; anything else is unclear.
patterns: Most episodes peaked around 18:00, 19:00 and 20:00, and 93% fell on weekdays, more than the 71% you'd expect, so they lean towards working days. The busiest month was Mar 2005 with 14 episodes.
